note_tweet.text:
A common assumption is that robots can learn from the huge amount of video already available on the internet.

But watching a human pick up a cup is not the same as giving a robot the information needed to reproduce that action.

Video mostly gives us pixels.

A robot needs much more: how the joints moved, where contact happened, how the object was manipulated, and what physical forces were involved.

That difference matters because Physical AI is not only about recognizing what is happening. It is about acting in the physical world.

A model can watch millions of videos of someone opening a door, but that does not automatically tell a robot how much force to apply, where its end-effector should make contact, or how its joints should coordinate.

This is why physical action data is fundamentally different from ordinary visual data.

The challenge is not simply finding more footage. It is capturing the structure of an action in a form that a robot can actually learn from.

That is also why simulation and real-world data become important parts of the Physical AI data stack.

The thesis is simple: pixels can describe an action, but actionable data needs to describe the physical interaction behind it.

@axisrobotics

note_tweet.text:
One of the biggest challenges in robotics is not just teaching a robot what to do. It is collecting enough useful data for it to learn.

In traditional workflows, collecting robot data can require physical hardware, human operators, controlled environments, and repeated demonstrations. Every new task or variation adds more work.

This creates a scaling problem. If better robots require more diverse experience, but collecting that experience depends heavily on physical setups, progress becomes expensive and slow.

The key question is how to make robot data generation more accessible and repeatable.

This is where digital twins and browser-based contribution become interesting. A task can be represented in a simulated environment, while contributors can generate robot trajectories without every interaction requiring direct operation of a physical robot.

The goal is not to eliminate physical robots. It is to reduce the dependence on physical hardware during the data-generation process, then use real-world deployment to evaluate results and identify what needs improvement.

For Physical AI, scaling intelligence may require scaling the process that produces training data.

The advantage will not come from collecting data once. It will come from building a repeatable system that can keep generating, improving, and validating useful data as new tasks emerge.

@axisrobotics

note_tweet.text:
One way to understand the robotics data problem is to look at where the data comes from.

A robot learning a new task needs more than a successful demonstration. It needs to understand the range of ways that task can happen.

The same object can appear in different positions. The environment can change. The camera angle can change. The robot can approach the task differently. And real-world edge cases are often exactly where a model fails.

This makes data diversity just as important as data volume.

A digital twin provides a useful starting point because a physical task can be represented in a controlled environment and then varied across many conditions.

Instead of collecting every variation directly from a physical robot, simulation can help generate a much wider set of possible scenarios before the data reaches the training stage.

The important thesis is not “simulation replaces the real world.”

It is that simulation can expand the data-generation process, while physical deployment provides the feedback needed to understand what actually works.

That creates a bridge between synthetic environments and physical robots.

More variation creates better coverage. Better coverage creates better training data. Better training data can improve deployment. And deployment creates new feedback for the next data cycle.

For Physical AI, the advantage may come from building this loop efficiently, not simply from building bigger models.

@axisrobotics

note_tweet.text:
A common assumption is that robots can learn from the huge amount of video already available on the internet.

But watching a human pick up a cup is not the same as giving a robot the information needed to reproduce that action.

Video mostly gives us pixels.

A robot needs much more: how the joints moved, where contact happened, how the object was manipulated, and what physical forces were involved.

That difference matters because Physical AI is not only about recognizing what is happening. It is about acting in the physical world.

A model can watch millions of videos of someone opening a door, but that does not automatically tell a robot how much force to apply, where its end-effector should make contact, or how its joints should coordinate.

This is why physical action data is fundamentally different from ordinary visual data.

The challenge is not simply finding more footage. It is capturing the structure of an action in a form that a robot can actually learn from.

That is also why simulation and real-world data become important parts of the Physical AI data stack.

The thesis is simple: pixels can describe an action, but actionable data needs to describe the physical interaction behind it.

@axisrobotics
